                    ### Question
                    A 67-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus comes to the emergency department because of lightheadedness over the past 2 hours. He reports that he has had similar episodes of lightheadedness and palpitations over the past 3 days. His only medication is metformin. His pulse is 110/min and irregularly irregular. An ECG shows a variable R-R interval and absence of P waves. The patient undergoes transesophageal echocardiography. During the procedure, the tip of the ultrasound probe is angled posteriorly within the esophagus. This view is most helpful for evaluating which of the following conditions?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Thrombus in the left pulmonary artery
opb. Myxoma in the left atrium
opc. Aneurysm of the descending aorta
opd. Thrombus in the left ventricular apex
ope. Tumor in the right main bronchus

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) is particularly useful for visualizing cardiac structures, especially in the left atrium where myxomas, a common type of cardiac tumor, are typically located. The angled posterior view during TEE enhances the visualization of the left atrium, making it optimal for diagnosing left atrial myxoma. This aligns with the consensus that TEE provides clearer images than transthoracic echocardiography and is effective in detecting cardiac masses. Therefore, the most relevant option is the evaluation of a myxoma in the left atrium.
